issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Trauma Cues: Comments on sexual violence
issues.explanation: For a patient whose index trauma is witnessing domestic violence in childhood, sexual-trauma-specific trigger content is a poor fit unless sexual violence was part of the witnessed events. Nothing else in the profile links the trauma memory or threat meanings to sexual content, so this item is hard to reconcile with the stated trauma type.

Avoiding sex is similarly trauma-content-specific and is not supported by the rest of the trigger, threat, or memory items for witnessed childhood domestic violence. In combination with the sexual-trauma trigger item, it suggests a different trauma theme than the one provided, making the profile clinically incoherent.

vignette:
Kareem Haddad is a 41-year-old single Lebanese-American construction worker who presented for his first psychological consultation after what he described, with visible reluctance, as "finally running out of other options." He has spent the better part of three decades managing the aftermath of what he witnessed as a child, and it is only now, with his functioning visibly narrowing, that he has allowed himself to sit in a therapist's office and attempt to account for it.

Kareem grew up in a household in Dearborn, Michigan, in which his father's rages were a recurring and unpredictable feature of domestic life. The violence he witnessed was not occasional - it was cyclical and escalating. What lodged most deeply in Kareem's memory, however, was a specific night when he was approximately nine years old. His father had come home late, and Kareem had been in the hallway when the argument began. He remembers with photographic precision the way his mother's back was pressed against the kitchen wall, the overhead light flickering, the particular angle of his father's raised arm. Other moments from that night are simply gone - blank spaces where memory should be - and when Kareem tries to deliberately reconstruct the sequence of events, he finds himself unable to access them in any ordered way. The images arrive not as narrative but as stills: isolated, vivid, and stripped of context. What he cannot retrieve deliberately arrives unbidden at other times, uninvited and complete.

In the years that followed, Kareem learned to read rooms. He became extraordinarily attentive to the faces of the men around him - foremen, co-workers, strangers on job sites - scanning for the particular tightening around the jaw, the shift in posture, the quality of stillness that in his childhood had preceded violence. On a construction site this vigilance is constant, and it exhausts him. When a delivery runs late or a subcontractor fails to show on schedule, Kareem does not interpret the delay as logistical - he is certain, in those moments, that something has gone wrong in a more fundamental sense, that the silence before the disruption is the same silence he once stood in at the end of that hallway. His body responds accordingly: his chest tightens, his hands become unsteady, and he has on several occasions had to remove himself from the work floor without explanation.

He avoids confrontation with a discipline that has shaped his entire social world. When disputes arise on site - over materials, timelines, or the ordinary friction of men working in close quarters - Kareem goes quiet and withdraws. He has turned down two supervisory positions over the past six years because he understood, correctly, that the role would require him to manage conflict directly. When police officers appear near a job site, as they occasionally do in the neighbourhoods where he works, he experiences an acute physical response and finds reasons to position himself elsewhere until they leave. He has come to believe that his body simply cannot tolerate the presence of authority in uniform without treating it as a precursor to harm.

In the evenings, Kareem drifts. He describes it as going somewhere else - a private interior space that is neither sleep nor fantasy exactly, but a retreat from the present into something quieter. He also finds himself dwelling on who he was before the weight of all this became so apparent to him: a younger version of himself who laughed more easily, who had been briefly engaged in his early thirties before the relationship ended under the strain of his withdrawal. He does not talk about the future with any ease. When a colleague recently asked him what he planned to do when the current project wrapped up, Kareem felt his throat close. The future, he has come to feel, is not a place he can safely imagine occupying.

What brought him in, finally, was a moment on site last month when a foreman raised his voice during a scheduling dispute. Kareem did not respond. He walked to his truck and sat there for forty minutes, shaking, unable to account for himself to anyone, including himself. He is hoping, he said carefully, to understand why a grown man is still standing in that hallway.
